text: From Descartes to the present, reason has been prized in Western culture, standing as the chief virtue of the modernist world view. <break time="0.8s" /> As we are led to believe, it is the power to reason that sets humans above the remainder of the animal kingdom, and is essential for human survival. <break time="0.8s" /> Literary study suggests otherwise. <break time="0.8s" /> Among the most important objections are those of the French literary theorist Jacques Derrida. <break time="0.8s" /> Derridas writings, often identified as deconstructionist, are ambiguous and open to many interpretations. <break time="0.8s" /> From one perspective, however, they significantly undermine the cultural investment in human reason. <break time="0.8s" /> Consider two major premises. <break time="0.8s" /> First, suggests Derrida, rational arguments bring about a massive suppression of meaning. <break time="0.8s" /> Broadly put, when we are convinced by a rational argument we do not know more, but less. <break time="0.8s" /> Second, if closely examined, all rational arguments will collapse. <break time="0.8s" /> Rationality, then, is not a foundation for anything, for our institutions of government and science, for example, or as a way of deciding on what is moral or worthwhile. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather, Derrida suggests, our good reasons are in the end both suppressive and empty.
